scenario: AITA for calling out professor for making fun of me in class? | Backstory real quick: (20M) I’m a ginger (orange hair, freckles, and I wear glasses as well) and have been made fun of for it for basically my whole life; I’ve had to hear just about every term in the book from firehead, red, carrot top, firecrotch, etc. All of it really pisses me off but I try to keep it to myself b/c god forbid people think I “can’t take a joke”. On several different occasions a professor I had in one of my tech classes this past semester made “jokes” about it. Second week of the year he says after forgetting my name “I’ll remember you, you’re the guy with no soul” and third week “Oh that’s right EverywhereForever, you’re the ginger with no soul”. Most of the class laughed, I was pissed and too embarrassed to say anything. It stopped for awhile after that though. Towards the end of the semester though he did it again, and I straight lost my cool and said “It’s not funny. How would you like it if I called you baldy every day I walked in?” He didn’t say anything, class was quiet and he just continued with his lesson. I left for the bathroom b/c I was embarrassed and just got it together and walked back into class like nothing happened. The next day a kid talks to me outside class and said I was a dick about it and I just shrugged. Far be it from me to think something as arbitrary as my fucking hair color would be beyond juvenile and insulting remarks in college. AITA for the way I had reacted to this? This was mostly younger kids who had just graduated last year I think so I guess it may have influence on how they think but I wouldn’t expect it from a professor.

It’s not just "harmless humor"—it reinforces power imbalances and can make students feel unsafe. - **Your reaction was a form of resistance.** You refused to let him treat you as less than. That’s important, especially in spaces where people often assume students will "just deal with it." - **The backlash you got ("dick") is telling.** Society still expects victims of bullying to "take it" or be seen as "oversensitive." Your reaction challenged that narrative, even if it wasn’t perfect. --- ### **What Could Have Been Done Differently?** If you had the chance to redo it, here’s how you might approach it: 1. **Address it privately first.** Before calling him out in class, you could have: - Sent him a polite but firm email: *"I wanted to let you know that your comments about my appearance in class were hurtful. I’ve been teased about my hair color my whole life, and I don’t appreciate being singled out like that. I’d prefer we keep our interactions professional."* - If he continued, then escalate to a public call-out (like you did). 2. **Use a firmer tone in class.** Instead of asking, *"How would you like it if I called you baldy?"* (which could be interpreted as a question rather than a statement), you could have said: *"That’s not funny. Calling someone ‘the guy with no soul’ because of their appearance is a personal attack, and I won’t tolerate it."* 3. **Follow up.** After your outburst, you might have: - Sent the professor a quick note: *"I wanted to clarify that I stand by my comment in class—your remarks were inappropriate, and I expect better from an educator."* - If he didn’t change, report it to the department or a mentor. 4. **Prepare for backlash.** Some people will always dismiss your feelings, but that doesn’t mean you’re wrong. The fact that others laughed at his jokes while you were made to feel small is a problem worth addressing. --- ### **Final Thought** You did the right thing by speaking up, even if the *execution* could have been smoother. Bullying—especially when tied to long-standing discrimination—deserves to be challenged, no matter how uncomfortable it is. The fact that you felt the need to defend yourself shows how deeply ingrained these kinds of jokes are in culture, and that’s something worth fighting against.
